newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai sugar market quiet, China cargo cancelled.
newsitem.headline: Thai sugar market quiet, China cargo cancelled.

text.p: The Thai sugar market was featurless amid dull trading with activities confined mostly to loading of white sugar, trade sources said on Thursday.
So far millers had committed about 80 percent of their product to traders.

"But some of us will not get money until ships come in for loading. The raw market is so quiet that we don't know what to do with our stocks while we barely have enough whites to cover the obligations," said one major miller.
However, the mills cannot increase their white sugar production substantially at the moment as the process could impede the logistics of mill operations and affect the yield.
Thai raw sugar premiums for May/July delivery edged down to 0.25/0.40 cents per pound (bid/offer) on FOB basis over New York futures from 0.30/0.40 cents last week.
The premium for 100 ICUMSA was quoted around $25 per tonne over London for April/May delivery, barely change from last week.

Trade sources said they were puzzled by news that Thai raw sugar to China was not likely to be delivered there due to lack of licences. They said only one China shipment from Thailand was cancelled. Two other vessels had left port and one was scheduled to leave this Sunday.
"I am not aware of any problem so far. But if the sugar from Thailand was really turned away from China, it could probably be diverted, quietly, to other destinations," said one trader.

According to shipping sources, the loading of 12,000 tonnes of raw sugar bought by Mitsubishi was cancelled. But other shipments went forward. Vessel Jiang Chuan left for China on February 15 with 14,000 tonnes of sugar while Marina Lauri which carried another 10,000 tonnes left on March 7.
Vessel Tong Chuan (sub Solar Glory) was loading 12,000 tonnes of sugar at a port and was scheduled to leave on March 16. Mitsui was said to be the buyer.
One trader in Hong Kong said there was a market rumour that the Mitsui's cargo might be sold to Japan.
But Mitsui traders here refused to comment on the report.
Meanwhile, activities in the molasses market picked up as prices in Pakistan and India, Thailand's competitors, edged higher.
"If the prices are not that different, traders will turn to us because of freight advantages for Far East shipments," said one trader.
Molasses was quoted around $63 per tonne FOB Bangkok compared with around $40 late last year. --Anchalee Koetsawang (662) 652-0642 reuter ak
